title: National Strategy for Artificial Intelligence #AIforAll
issuing_body: NITI Aayog
summary: The founding document of India's AI policy journey - a discussion paper prepared by NITI Aayog under a Union Budget 2018-19 mandate, branding India's approach as #AIforAll. It identifies five priority sectors (healthcare, agriculture, education, smart cities, smart mobility) and proposes Centres of Excellence for AI research, large-scale reskilling, annotated public datasets, and a national data marketplace. Not binding, but nearly every subsequent central and state AI initiative traces its framing back to this paper.
who_it_applies_to: Non-binding strategy paper. Primarily a reference for central ministries, state governments, researchers, and companies seeking to understand the origins and priorities of India's AI programme.
key_obligations: None - advisory. Recommends establishing ICTAI Centres of Excellence; aligning programmes to the five priority sectors; creating annotated datasets for public-interest AI; large-scale workforce reskilling; developing responsible AI guidelines.

title: Responsible AI for All - Part 1: Guiding Principles
issuing_body: NITI Aayog
summary: First instalment of NITI Aayog's Responsible AI approach papers, establishing seven principles for responsible AI derived from the Constitution of India: safety and reliability, equality, inclusivity and non-discrimination, privacy and security, transparency, accountability, and protection of positive human values. It analyses systems-level risks such as explainability gaps, exclusion and accountability failures, and includes a self-assessment guide. These principles remain the most-cited ethical baseline in Indian AI policy, echoed in later sectoral frameworks.
who_it_applies_to: Non-binding guidance for government agencies and for AI developers and deployers across the public and private sectors.
key_obligations: Voluntary. Recommends adopting the seven principles across design, development and deployment; conducting risk-proportionate impact assessments; documenting AI systems against each principle.

title: Responsible AI for All - Part 2: Operationalising Responsible AI
issuing_body: NITI Aayog
summary: Companion paper to Part 1, focused on how to operationalise the seven responsible AI principles in practice. Provides sector-specific guidance and case studies for healthcare, agriculture, MSMEs and education, a risk-based assessment framework, and proposed enforcement mechanisms, and maps the roles of government, industry and research institutions in making responsible AI work in Indian organisational contexts.
who_it_applies_to: Non-binding guidance for AI developers and deploying organisations, particularly those using AI in social or governance contexts.
key_obligations: Voluntary. Recommends sector-specific risk and fairness assessments; deployment checklists; internal accountability mechanisms; documented AI decision trails.

title: IndiaAI Mission
issuing_body: Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology (MeitY)
summary: Cabinet-approved national programme with a Rs 10,371.92 crore outlay over five years - the financial and institutional engine of India's AI ambitions. Built on seven pillars: subsidised national GPU compute capacity, an Innovation Centre for indigenous foundation models, the AIKosh datasets platform, sectoral application development, FutureSkills training, startup financing, and Safe and Trusted AI. Implemented by the IndiaAI Independent Business Division under Digital India Corporation; most subsequent governance initiatives, including the AI Governance Guidelines and the AI Safety Institute, sit under its umbrella.
who_it_applies_to: A government programme rather than a regulation. Relevant to AI startups, researchers and academic institutions seeking compute, data, funding or skilling support, and to government bodies deploying AI.
key_obligations: No compliance obligations - participation-based. Startups and researchers can access subsidised GPU compute via the IndiaAI Compute Portal, datasets via AIKosh, FutureSkills programmes, and startup financing through the fund of funds.

title: Digital Personal Data Protection Act 2023
issuing_body: Ministry of Law and Justice
summary: India's first comprehensive data protection law, governing the processing of digital personal data - including the data that trains and feeds AI systems. It establishes consent and notice requirements, rights for individuals (Data Principals), obligations for organisations (Data Fiduciaries) including breach notification and erasure, and a Data Protection Board with penalty powers up to Rs 250 crore. Enforcement depends on the DPDP Rules 2025, which phase in core obligations through 2027. For AI builders, this is the binding legal baseline for any system touching personal data of Indian residents.
who_it_applies_to: Binding law. All government and private entities processing digital personal data of individuals in India, or offering goods and services to Indian residents from abroad. Limited exemptions for personal use, notified state instrumentalities, and research.
key_obligations: Obtain valid consent or rely on listed legitimate uses; provide notice before collection; allow easy consent withdrawal; implement reasonable security safeguards; notify the Board and affected individuals of breaches; erase data when its purpose ends; verifiable parental consent for under-18s with no tracking or targeted advertising aimed at children; Significant Data Fiduciaries must appoint an India-based DPO and independent auditor and conduct periodic impact assessments.

title: Advisory on Due Diligence and Identification of AI-Generated Deepfakes (December 2023)
issuing_body: Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology (MeitY)
summary: MeitY advisory (No. 2(4)/2023-CyberLaws-2) directing all intermediaries to act against AI-generated deepfakes and synthetic misinformation, issued amid high-profile deepfake incidents in late 2023. It instructs platforms not to permit AI-generated content unlawful under Rule 3(1)(b) of the IT Rules 2021, to embed permanent metadata in synthetic content enabling traceability to creator and originator, and to prevent AI-enabled bias or threats to electoral integrity, on pain of losing safe harbour under Section 79 of the IT Act. Effectively the first step toward the binding deepfake framework added to the IT Rules in February 2026.
who_it_applies_to: All intermediaries and platforms operating in India, including social media, messaging and OTT platforms and providers of generative AI tools.
key_obligations: Prevent unlawful AI-generated content; embed permanent metadata or identifiers in synthetic content for traceability; prevent AI-enabled bias, discrimination and electoral interference; submit an action-taken report within 15 days; maintain Section 79 due diligence.

title: Advisory to Intermediaries on AI Compliance and Unreliable AI Models (March 2024)
issuing_body: Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology (MeitY)
summary: Follow-up MeitY advisory (No. 2(4)/2023-CyberLaws-3) issued after observed non-compliance with the December 2023 deepfake advisory - and the most controversial of the AI advisories. As issued on 1 March 2024 it required under-tested or unreliable AI models to obtain explicit Government of India permission before being made available to Indian users; after strong industry pushback, a revised advisory on 15 March 2024 withdrew the approval requirement in favour of labelling under-tested models and outputs. Other requirements - consent popups disclosing output fallibility, user warnings about unlawful AI content, and permanent metadata in synthetic media - were retained.
who_it_applies_to: All intermediaries and platforms hosting or enabling AI, ML, LLM or generative AI functionality for users in India.
key_obligations: As revised on 15 March 2024: label under-tested or unreliable AI models and their outputs; display consent popups disclosing the fallibility of AI outputs; prevent unlawful AI-generated content and electoral interference; inform users of consequences of dealing in unlawful AI content; embed permanent metadata for deepfake attribution. The original requirement of prior government permission was withdrawn.

title: Recommendations on Leveraging Artificial Intelligence and Big Data in Telecommunication Sector
issuing_body: Telecom Regulatory Authority of India (TRAI)
summary: TRAI's recommendations to the government on leveraging AI and big data in telecom, most consequential for what goes beyond telecom: it proposes an independent statutory body, the Artificial Intelligence and Data Authority of India (AIDAI), to govern AI across all sectors through a risk-based framework - one of the earliest official calls for dedicated AI regulation in India. Telecom-specific recommendations cover AI in spectrum management, network optimisation, fraud detection and consumer protection.
who_it_applies_to: Recommendations to government, not binding rules. Addressed to the Department of Telecommunications and MeitY; relevant to telecom service providers and AI vendors serving the sector.
key_obligations: Non-binding. Recommends establishing AIDAI as a statutory cross-sectoral AI authority; risk-based regulation of AI use cases; a multi-stakeholder advisory body; measures to accelerate responsible AI adoption in telecom.

title: Ethical Guidelines for Application of Artificial Intelligence in Biomedical Research and Healthcare
issuing_body: Indian Council of Medical Research (ICMR)
summary: ICMR's ethical framework for AI in biomedical research and healthcare - the first sectoral AI ethics guidance from an Indian health authority. It sets ten patient-centric principles including autonomy, safety, privacy, accountability and trustworthiness, and walks through the ethics review process for AI health tools across clinical decision support, diagnostics, drug discovery and public health surveillance. Framed as a living document, it has become the reference standard cited in government health-AI deployments.
who_it_applies_to: Healthcare AI developers, clinical researchers, hospitals, ethics committees, and sponsors of AI-in-health research.
key_obligations: Obtain ethics committee clearance for AI healthcare tools; document training data and assess bias; obtain patient consent for AI use in care; conduct clinical validation; ensure human oversight of all AI-assisted clinical decisions.

title: Telemedicine Practice Guidelines
issuing_body: Ministry of Health and Family Welfare (MoHFW) / National Medical Commission
summary: India's legal framework for telemedicine, issued at the onset of COVID-19 under the Indian Medical Council professional conduct regulations, enabling registered medical practitioners to consult remotely. Its AI significance is a bright-line rule: AI and ML platforms may support practitioners but are explicitly prohibited from counselling patients or prescribing medicines - only a registered practitioner may do so. Also establishes consultation protocols, a four-tier drug prescription matrix tied to consultation mode, and record-keeping duties.
who_it_applies_to: Registered medical practitioners, telemedicine platforms, and health-tech companies offering remote consultations or symptom-checker services.
key_obligations: Verify practitioner and patient identity; obtain patient consent; assess whether telemedicine is appropriate; follow the drug prescription matrix (no Schedule X drugs or narcotics via telemedicine); maintain digital consultation records; platforms must verify practitioner registration and must not allow AI to counsel patients or prescribe.

title: Draft Guidance Document on Medical Device Software
issuing_body: Central Drugs Standard Control Organisation (CDSCO)
summary: Draft CDSCO guidance, opened for public comment, on how Medical Device Software - including AI and ML based diagnostic and clinical decision support tools - is regulated under the Medical Devices Rules 2017. It distinguishes Software in a Medical Device (SiMD) from standalone Software as a Medical Device (SaMD), and applies a four-class risk matrix (A to D) combining the significance of the clinical information provided with the seriousness of the healthcare situation. Once finalised, this will be the de facto licensing rulebook for health-AI products in India.
who_it_applies_to: Indian manufacturers and importers of medical device software, including developers of AI/ML diagnostic and therapeutic software and clinical decision support applications, under MDR 2017.
key_obligations: Draft stage - proposed obligations: classify software under the prescribed risk matrix; obtain manufacturing or import licences from the appropriate licensing authority; provide clinical evidence of safety and performance; implement an ISO 13485 compliant quality management system; conduct post-market surveillance and report adverse events.

title: Reimagining Agriculture: A Roadmap for Frontier Technology Led Transformation
issuing_body: NITI Aayog (Frontier Tech Hub)
summary: Strategic roadmap from NITI Aayog's Frontier Tech Hub (with CII, BCG, Google and EkStep Foundation) for technology-led transformation of Indian agriculture toward Viksit Bharat 2047. It segments farmers into three archetypes, diagnoses six systemic roadblocks - siloed data, trust deficits, the phygital divide, ecosystem fragmentation, and talent and capital gaps - and proposes a Digital Agriculture Mission 2.0 spanning a sovereign agri-data ecosystem (AgriKosh), AI-powered last-mile advisory via VISTAAR, mission-oriented R&D, and frontier-tech Centres of Excellence.
who_it_applies_to: Non-binding roadmap for agriculture and IT ministries, state agriculture departments, agritech startups and companies, research institutions, and farmer producer organisations.
key_obligations: None - advisory. Recommends an inter-ministerial committee for the AgriKosh data ecosystem; mapping and tracking of agritech accelerators; time-bound task forces on R&D and agri-talent; an NSQF-aligned agri-talent framework; integrating AI advisory channels with DPI such as AgriStack and VISTAAR.

title: Master Direction on Information Technology Governance, Risk, Controls and Assurance Practices
issuing_body: Reserve Bank of India (RBI)
summary: Binding RBI Master Direction on IT governance and risk for regulated financial entities, in force from April 2024. While not an AI-specific instrument, it is currently the closest thing to enforceable AI rules in Indian banking: it brings AI and ML models within IT and model risk governance, requiring board-level oversight, model inventories, periodic audits, and explainability for AI used in areas such as credit underwriting and fraud scoring.
who_it_applies_to: Binding on scheduled commercial banks, NBFCs above thresholds, and other RBI-regulated entities using technology - including AI and ML - in operations or customer-facing decisions.
key_obligations: Board-level IT strategy committee oversight; maintain an AI/ML model inventory with risk classification; conduct periodic model audits; implement explainability for AI-driven credit decisions; report AI-related incidents to RBI.

title: National Education Policy 2020
issuing_body: Ministry of Education (MoE)
summary: India's national education reform blueprint, with AI woven through its skilling and curriculum agenda: coding and computational thinking from Grade 6, AI integrated into school and higher-education curricula, AI-enabled personalised learning, and teacher upskilling in technology pedagogy. Not a regulation, but it drives the education-side pipeline that most AI skilling programmes - including IndiaAI FutureSkills - build on.
who_it_applies_to: Schools, universities, state education departments, teacher training institutions, and education technology companies.
key_obligations: Policy direction rather than obligations: introduce coding and AI literacy from middle school; restructure higher-education curricula for multidisciplinary learning; train teachers in technology and AI pedagogy; link vocational AI skilling to national credentials.

title: CERT-In Advisory on Best Practices for Generative AI Security (CIAD-2025-0013)
issuing_body: Indian Computer Emergency Response Team (CERT-In)
summary: CERT-In security advisory cataloguing the main attack vectors against generative AI systems - data poisoning, adversarial inputs, model inversion and model stealing, prompt injection, hallucination exploitation, and backdoor attacks - and recommending defensive practices for organisations and individual users. Advisory in nature, but CERT-In guidance feeds into the mandatory cyber incident reporting ecosystem under the IT Act, making this a practical security baseline for GenAI deployment in India.
who_it_applies_to: All organisations and individuals deploying or using generative AI tools, and AI application developers.
key_obligations: Advisory best practices: configure and periodically review GenAI access rights to organisational data; fact-check AI outputs and avoid sole reliance on AI for critical decisions; use strong authentication for AI service accounts; stay alert to AI-generated phishing and deepfakes.

title: Maharashtra Artificial Intelligence Policy 2026
issuing_body: Government of Maharashtra
summary: Maharashtra's first dedicated state AI policy, approved by the state cabinet on 29 April 2026 after development by a 16-member taskforce constituted in January 2025. It targets over Rs 10,000 crore of investment and 1.5 lakh jobs, and commits to six AI Centres of Excellence, five AI Innovation Cities, 12 AI incubators, a Rs 500 crore AI venture fund, 2,000 GPUs of state compute capacity, financial support for 5,000 MSMEs to adopt AI, and a Maharashtra AI Mission aligned with the national IndiaAI Mission. The full policy document and government resolution are awaited; this entry reflects the cabinet announcement.
who_it_applies_to: State government departments, AI companies and startups, MSMEs, and educational institutions in Maharashtra.
key_obligations: Programmatic commitments by the state government; incentive eligibility and participation details to follow publication of the policy document and operational guidelines.

title: Telangana Artificial Intelligence Framework 2020
issuing_body: Government of Telangana (ITE&C Department)
summary: Telangana's AI strategy framework, launched when the state declared 2020 its Year of AI, aiming to make Telangana a global AI hub. Built on six pillars - data exchange and high-performance computing, skilling, governance and ethics, research, adoption, and an AI-Innovestment social-good fund - and executed through T-AIM (Telangana AI Mission) in partnership with NASSCOM. Notably one of the few state policies with concrete data-ethics requirements: companies using government datasets must file compliance reports and complete mandatory data ethics training.
who_it_applies_to: Telangana state departments, AI companies and startups, research institutions, and any entity accessing state government datasets.
key_obligations: Companies accessing government datasets must submit compliance reports on ethical data use; employees of IT companies using government data must complete a mandatory data ethics course; government AI procurement must follow AI Ethics Group guidelines including explainability; government staff operating AI must be trained on its capabilities and limits; data providers on the open data platform must obtain certification.

title: Karnataka Artificial Intelligence Strategy
issuing_body: Government of Karnataka
summary: Karnataka has signalled a standalone AI strategy to formalise Bengaluru's position as a global AI hub, building on AI references across its IT Policy 2020-25, Startup Policy 2022-27 and the Karnataka Digital Economy Mission. No dedicated AI policy document has been released yet; this entry tracks the announcement.
who_it_applies_to: State departments, IT companies, startups, global capability centres, and research institutions in Karnataka - once released.
key_obligations: Details pending finalisation.

title: Tamil Nadu Safe and Ethical Artificial Intelligence Policy 2020
issuing_body: Government of Tamil Nadu (Information Technology Department)
summary: The most operationally specific state AI policy in India: Tamil Nadu mandates an ethical evaluation gate for every AI system the state government procures or deploys. Its TAM-DEF framework and DEEP-MAX scorecard rate systems across transparency, fairness, privacy, misuse protection and related dimensions before public rollout, with scores to be recorded on a tamper-proof blockchain (ACTS) and refreshed every six months. Oversight sits with a committee chaired by the Chief Secretary, with TNeGA's emerging-technologies centre (CEET) as technical adviser.
who_it_applies_to: All Tamil Nadu government bodies, public sector undertakings, boards, cooperatives, and government-controlled or government-aided entities procuring or deploying AI.
key_obligations: Consult CEET at TNeGA before any AI procurement; evaluate all AI systems on the DEEP-MAX scorecard before deployment and meet acceptability thresholds; record scores on the ACTS blockchain (or interim mechanism) and refresh at least every six months; accept the government's right to recall AI applications that fall below thresholds.

title: AI in Indian Defence: A Compendium of AI-Based Products and Technologies
issuing_body: Department of Defence Production, Ministry of Defence
summary: A showcase compendium from the Department of Defence Production cataloguing AI products and technologies developed across India's defence ecosystem - DRDO, defence PSUs, private companies and startups. It spans autonomous systems, swarm drones, cognitive radar, maritime anomaly detection, surveillance and facial recognition, cybersecurity, logistics, and lethal autonomous weapon systems. Not a policy instrument, but the most complete public picture of where Indian defence AI capability stands.
who_it_applies_to: Reference document for defence industry, armed forces, DRDO, and policymakers involved in defence AI procurement and capability development.
key_obligations: None - informational compendium. Featured products remain subject to defence procurement procedures, export controls, and technology transfer agreements.

title: National Digital Health Mission: Health Data Management Policy
issuing_body: Ministry of Health and Family Welfare (MoHFW) / NDHM
summary: The data governance backbone of India's digital health ecosystem (now ABDM), establishing privacy-by-design rules for personal health data - the raw material of health AI. It defines roles across the federated ecosystem (health information providers and users, consent managers, processors), creates the Health ID and the professional and facility registries, and sets a granular consent framework with rights to access, correct, erase and port health data. It also prohibits denial of health services for refusing to create a Health ID.
who_it_applies_to: All entities in the National Digital Health Ecosystem: hospitals, diagnostic centres, insurers, health-tech and pharmaceutical companies, researchers, and consent managers handling personal health data.
key_obligations: Process health data only with free, informed, specific and revocable consent; implement privacy by design and publish the policy; apply security practices including encryption and de-identification; conduct impact assessments before high-risk processing; maintain audit trails; appoint a DPO and grievance officer with one-month response times; report breaches to NDHM; anonymise data before secondary use.

title: Enabling Framework for Regulatory Sandbox
issuing_body: Reserve Bank of India (RBI)
summary: RBI's framework allowing fintech innovations - including AI-driven credit scoring, lending and payments products - to be live-tested with real customers under relaxed regulatory norms within a supervised boundary. First issued in August 2019 and updated most recently on 28 February 2024, when cohorts became theme-neutral, testing windows were extended to nine months, and compliance with the DPDP Act 2023 was made a condition of participation. Several AI-in-finance proofs of concept have come through its cohorts.
who_it_applies_to: Fintech companies, banks partnering with fintechs, and AI-based lending, insurance and payments platforms seeking to test products before full regulatory compliance.
key_obligations: Apply to an RBI sandbox cohort with product details and risk assessment; operate strictly within the approved testing boundary; test only with consenting customers; comply with the DPDP Act 2023; submit an outcome report to RBI at the end of the cohort.

title: Consultation Paper on Guidelines for Responsible Usage of AI/ML in Indian Securities Markets
issuing_body: Securities and Exchange Board of India (SEBI)
summary: SEBI consultation paper proposing India's first dedicated guidelines for responsible AI and ML use across securities markets, building on its existing AI reporting requirements and IOSCO's framework. It proposes five core principles - model governance, investor protection and disclosure, testing frameworks, fairness and bias controls, and data privacy and cybersecurity - with a lighter regime for internal, non-customer-facing AI. Comments closed in July 2025; read alongside the February 2025 Intermediaries Amendment, which already makes regulated entities legally responsible for their AI tools.
who_it_applies_to: All SEBI-regulated participants using AI/ML: exchanges, clearing corporations, depositories, brokers, mutual funds, portfolio managers, investment advisers, and their AI vendors.
key_obligations: Proposed (consultation stage): skilled internal model-oversight teams with senior management accountability; pre-deployment and shadow testing in segregated environments; continuous monitoring with results shared with SEBI; independent audits; customer disclosure of AI use, risks and accuracy; bias identification and removal; data governance and breach reporting.

title: India AI Governance Guidelines
issuing_body: Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology (MeitY)
summary: India's first comprehensive national framework for AI governance, prepared by a MeitY-constituted expert committee and released in November 2025. Rather than proposing a new AI law, it adopts a light-touch, principle-based approach anchored in seven guiding sutras - including Trust is the Foundation, People First, and Innovation over Restraint - and takes the position that existing laws (IT Act, DPDP Act, consumer protection, copyright) already address most AI harms. Its key structural move is institutional: it recommends an AI Governance Group for inter-ministerial coordination, a Technology and Policy Expert Committee, an AI Safety Institute, and an AI incident database.
who_it_applies_to: Non-binding guidance, not law. Directly relevant to anyone developing or deploying AI systems in India, to sectoral regulators (RBI, SEBI, ICMR and others) designing domain-specific rules, and to ministries. Creates no enforceable obligations, but signals the direction of future Indian AI regulation.
key_obligations: Voluntary. Industry actors are guided to comply with all applicable Indian laws and demonstrate compliance when called upon by regulators; establish accessible, multilingual grievance-redressal mechanisms; and maintain transparency across the AI value chain. Regulators are guided toward proportionate, flexible, periodically reviewed frameworks rather than command-and-control rules.

title: National AI Strategy for Skilling and Workforce Development
issuing_body: Ministry of Skill Development and Entrepreneurship (MSDE)
summary: A forthcoming national strategy to prepare India's workforce for an AI-driven economy through sector skill councils and the integration of AI and ML modules into ITI and polytechnic curricula. Expected to define national AI occupational standards, create a registry of certified AI trainers, and link skilling outcomes to AI industry employment. No document has been published yet; this entry tracks the announcement.
who_it_applies_to: Sector skill councils, training partners, employers in AI-intensive industries, and ITI and polytechnic institutions - once released.
key_obligations: Details pending publication.

title: Information Technology (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Rules, 2021 (as amended to 6 April 2023)
issuing_body: Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology (MeitY)
summary: The core subordinate legislation under the IT Act governing intermediaries and digital media in India - the legal scaffolding on which all of MeitY's AI and deepfake obligations hang. It sets due diligence duties for all intermediaries (prohibited content categories, grievance timelines, takedown and preservation duties), heavier obligations for Significant Social Media Intermediaries (India-resident compliance officers, traceability, proactive CSAM detection), an online gaming framework, and a three-tier ethics code for digital news and OTT platforms. This entry covers the consolidated text as amended to April 2023; the February 2026 amendment adding the synthetic media framework is tracked as a separate entry.
who_it_applies_to: All intermediaries operating in India, Significant Social Media Intermediaries above notified thresholds, online gaming intermediaries, and publishers of news and OTT content.
key_obligations: Publish rules and privacy policy in Indian languages; prevent listed categories of unlawful content; acknowledge grievances within 24 hours and resolve within 15 days; preserve removed content for 180 days; respond to government requests within 72 hours; SSMIs must appoint India-resident compliance officers, publish monthly compliance reports, and enable originator traceability on lawful orders.

title: Strengthening AI Governance Through Techno-Legal Framework
issuing_body: Office of the Principal Scientific Adviser to the Government of India
summary: White paper from the Office of the Principal Scientific Adviser arguing that India's AI governance should be techno-legal: embedding compliance into AI systems through technical mechanisms - watermarking, bias detection, privacy-enhancing technologies, responsible-AI firewalls, agent kill-switches - rather than relying only on after-the-fact enforcement. It maps risks and controls across five AI lifecycle stages from data collection to agentic AI, and details the institutional machinery (AI Governance Group chaired by the PSA, an expert committee within MeitY, an AI Safety Institute, and a national AI incident database) that operationalises the AI Governance Guidelines.
who_it_applies_to: Non-binding. AI developers and deployers, sectoral regulators designing AI frameworks, ministries deploying AI in public services, and researchers building responsible-AI tools.
key_obligations: Recommended practices: techno-legal governance teams with board-level accountability; impact assessments before training on personal data; privacy-enhancing technologies and fairness assessment; red-teaming and model scoring before deployment; runtime monitoring and AI firewalls at inference; behaviour logging and kill switches for agentic AI; participation in national AI incident reporting once established.

title: Rajasthan Artificial Intelligence and Machine Learning Policy 2026
issuing_body: Government of Rajasthan
summary: Rajasthan's dedicated AI/ML policy, approved by the state cabinet in December 2025 and unveiled on 6 January 2026 at the Rajasthan DigiFest in Jaipur. Operative for five years, it works as a top-up incentive layer: entities eligible under the state's base policies (RIPS 2024, MSME Policy 2024, Startup Policy 2022, Data Centre Policy 2025) receive additional fiscal and non-fiscal incentives for AI activities undertaken within Rajasthan - covering AI development, model training, R&D units, data centres and compute infrastructure. It also commits to AI cloud services, secure data repositories, testing platforms, and AI education across schools, ITIs, polytechnics and colleges, with an emphasis on ethical and responsible AI.
who_it_applies_to: Manufacturing and services industries, MSMEs and startups, R&D units, data centre and compute providers, academic institutions, and government departments undertaking AI activities in Rajasthan.
key_obligations: Incentive-based rather than regulatory: only AI activities initiated after notification and located within Rajasthan qualify; eligibility follows the criteria of the relevant base (parent) policy; incentives are top-ups subject to amendments and clarifications by the state government.

title: MahaAgri-AI Policy 2025-2029
issuing_body: Agriculture Department, Government of Maharashtra
summary: Maharashtra's sectoral policy for AI in agriculture, with an initial Rs 500 crore allocation - the first dedicated state agri-AI policy in India. Built around eight pillars including an AI and Agritech Innovation Centre, a federated Agriculture Data Exchange (ADeX) with consent-based access, a shared AI remote-sensing and geospatial engine for crop and drought intelligence, GenAI-powered multilingual farmer advisory (VISTAAR), blockchain-based agri-export traceability, and differentiated support for agritech startups. Governed by a State-Level Steering Committee, with technical and commercial vetting of every funded project.
who_it_applies_to: Maharashtra's agriculture department and district administrations, agritech companies and startups, State Agriculture Universities, farmer producer organisations, exporters and certification agencies.
key_obligations: Solution providers must route proposals through the Innovation Centre and pass technical and commercial feasibility evaluation; ADeX users must follow consent-driven access and state data governance rules; AI deployed in government schemes must meet responsible AI and privacy standards; all interventions face KPI-linked monitoring and third-party impact assessment.

title: Responsible AI for All: Adopting the Framework - A Use Case Approach on Facial Recognition Technology
issuing_body: NITI Aayog (research by Vidhi Centre for Legal Policy)
summary: Third paper in NITI Aayog's Responsible AI series, stress-testing the seven responsible AI principles against a live use case: facial recognition technology. It surveys how FRT works, its design-based and rights-based risks, and global regulation, then evaluates the Digi Yatra biometric airport boarding system against each principle - producing concrete recommendations on consent, data minimisation, bias testing and human review that apply to any FRT deployment in India.
who_it_applies_to: Government and private entities deploying facial recognition, airport operators using biometric boarding, and law enforcement agencies using automated FRT.
key_obligations: Non-binding recommendations: voluntary and informed consent for FRT; demographic bias and accuracy testing before deployment; strict data minimisation and retention limits; grievance mechanisms for affected individuals; human review of FRT alerts before any consequential action.

title: Framework for Responsible and Ethical Enablement of Artificial Intelligence in the Financial Sector (FREE-AI)
issuing_body: Reserve Bank of India (RBI) - FREE-AI Committee
summary: Report of the RBI-constituted committee (chaired by Prof. Pushpak Bhattacharyya, IIT Bombay) on enabling AI in the financial sector responsibly - the most detailed sectoral AI framework any Indian regulator has produced. It sets seven guiding sutras (later mirrored in MeitY's national guidelines) and 26 recommendations across six pillars, pairing innovation enablers - financial-sector data infrastructure, an AI sandbox, indigenous financial AI models, graded liability - with risk controls including board-approved AI policies, red-teaming of higher-risk systems, AI incident reporting, audits and disclosure. The recommendations await operationalisation through formal RBI guidance.
who_it_applies_to: All RBI-regulated entities - banks, NBFCs, payment system operators, fintechs - plus financial regulators, industry bodies, and third-party AI vendors serving the sector.
key_obligations: Recommendations pending formal RBI directions: board-approved AI policy; data and model lifecycle governance aligned with the DPDP Act; AI-specific product approval; consumer protection with AI disclosure; red-teaming of medium and high-risk AI at least semi-annually; AI incident reporting; semi-annually updated model inventories; AI disclosures in annual reports; risk-based internal and third-party audits.

title: Transforming Healthcare Delivery Through Artificial Intelligence
issuing_body: PIB Research Unit, Press Information Bureau
summary: PIB Research Unit report published ahead of the India-AI Impact Summit 2026, documenting how AI has been deployed across India's public health system from 2022 to 2025: AI chest X-ray screening for TB, the MadhuNetrAI diabetic retinopathy programme, AI clinical decision support within eSanjeevani's 282 million teleconsultations, cancer imaging biobanks, fraud detection in AB-PMJAY, and AI-driven disease surveillance. Not a policy instrument, but a useful official record of deployment scale - and it confirms MoHFW is developing a sector-specific Strategy for AI in Healthcare for India (SAHI).
who_it_applies_to: Reference document for health ministries, the National Health Authority, health-AI companies, and researchers tracking government health-AI deployment.
key_obligations: None - informational. Notes that health-AI deployments are expected to follow ICMR's 2023 ethical guidelines and MeitY's AI Governance Guidelines.

title: Digital Personal Data Protection Rules 2025
issuing_body: Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology (MeitY)
summary: The implementing rules that bring the DPDP Act 2023 to life, notified on 13 November 2025 with phased commencement: Data Protection Board governance immediately, Consent Managers from late 2026, and core obligations - notice, security safeguards, breach reporting, erasure, children's data verification - around May 2027. They specify what compliance actually looks like: itemised standalone notices, minimum security measures, 72-hour breach reports to the Board, three-year inactivity erasure for large platforms, DigiLocker-based parental consent verification, and annual impact assessments for Significant Data Fiduciaries. The compliance clock for India's AI and data ecosystem now runs on these dates.
who_it_applies_to: All Data Fiduciaries and processors covered by the DPDP Act; Consent Managers seeking registration; Significant Data Fiduciaries; and large e-commerce, online gaming and social media platforms under the Third Schedule.
key_obligations: Phased: itemised plain-language notice before consent; minimum security safeguards including encryption or tokenisation, access controls and one-year log retention; breach notification to affected individuals without delay and a full report to the Board within 72 hours; erasure when purpose ends, with a three-year inactivity rule and 48-hour warning for large platforms; verifiable parental consent for children via identity checks or DigiLocker tokens; 90-day grievance response; Significant Data Fiduciaries must conduct annual impact assessments and audits and may face data localisation directions.

title: IT (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Amendment Rules 2026 - Synthetically Generated Information
issuing_body: Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology (MeitY)
summary: The fourth major amendment to the IT Rules 2021 and India's first binding law on AI-generated content. It defines synthetically generated information (SGI) - AI-created or altered media that could pass as real - and requires platforms offering synthetic-media tools to block creation of harmful SGI, prominently label all lawful AI-generated content, and embed permanent provenance metadata that users cannot remove. Significant social media intermediaries must additionally collect and verify user declarations of AI-generated content. Enforcement timelines tighten sharply across the Rules: takedown orders within 3 hours, non-consensual intimate imagery within 2 hours, and grievances resolved within 7 days.
who_it_applies_to: All intermediaries serving Indian users, with specific duties for any platform offering tools to create or modify synthetic content - generative AI image, video and audio tools included - and additional duties for significant social media intermediaries.
key_obligations: Deploy automated tools to block creation of unlawful SGI (CSAM, intimate imagery, false documents, deceptive depictions of real people or events); label all permissible SGI as AI-generated with embedded permanent metadata and identifiers; prohibit removal or suppression of labels; SSMIs must require and verify user declarations of synthetic content; remove content on takedown orders within 3 hours and NCII within 2 hours; resolve grievances within 7 days; remind users of obligations at least quarterly.

title: SEBI (Intermediaries) (Amendment) Regulations 2025 - Usage of Artificial Intelligence
issuing_body: Securities and Exchange Board of India (SEBI)
summary: A short but consequential amendment inserting Chapter IIIB (Regulation 16C) into the SEBI Intermediaries Regulations 2008 - the first binding, cross-cutting AI rule in Indian securities law. Any SEBI-regulated entity using AI or ML tools, whether built in-house or procured from vendors and regardless of the scale of adoption, is made solely responsible for the privacy, security and integrity of investor data, for the outputs of those tools, and for compliance with applicable law. Parallel amendments applied the same principle to stock exchanges, clearing corporations and depositories. Notified on 6 February 2025 and in force from 10 February 2025.
who_it_applies_to: Binding on every person regulated by SEBI that uses AI/ML tools - brokers, mutual funds, portfolio managers, investment advisers, merchant bankers and others - whether the tools are developed in-house or procured from third parties.
key_obligations: Sole responsibility for the privacy, security and integrity of investor and stakeholder data processed by AI/ML tools; sole responsibility for outputs relied upon or dealt with; compliance with all applicable laws; exposure to SEBI enforcement action under Chapter V for violations.

title: Odisha Artificial Intelligence Policy 2025
issuing_body: Government of Odisha (Electronics & IT Department)
summary: Odisha's state AI policy, issued as a government resolution by the Electronics and IT Department on 18 June 2025. It directs AI adoption toward five focus areas - healthcare, education, agriculture, disaster management and governance - supported by strategy tracks on infrastructure, skills, energy and policy. Implementation instruments span compute and data infrastructure, an innovation centre, AI in school and higher education, workforce and government-official skilling, clean energy for AI, ethical use guidelines, data governance and cybersecurity, executed in three phases through a dedicated Odisha AI Mission and taskforce.
who_it_applies_to: Odisha state departments, AI companies and startups, academic institutions, and partners participating in the Odisha AI Mission.
key_obligations: Programmatic state commitments rather than regulatory obligations; AI deployments are to follow the policy's ethical use guidelines, data governance and cybersecurity requirements, with implementation overseen by the AI Mission Taskforce and an AI cell in the E&IT Department.

title: Artificial Intelligence (Ethics and Accountability) Bill 2025
issuing_body: Lok Sabha (Private Member's Bill)
summary: A Private Member's Bill introduced in the Lok Sabha in December 2025 proposing binding AI accountability legislation: a statutory AI Ethics Committee, mandatory ethical reviews for high-risk and surveillance systems, bias audits, developer obligations, restrictions on certain AI uses in law enforcement and employment, grievance mechanisms, and penalties up to Rs 5 crore. Private Members' Bills rarely pass, but it signals parliamentary appetite for binding AI accountability and may influence future legislation.
who_it_applies_to: If enacted: AI developers and deployers across sectors, with heightened obligations for high-risk, surveillance, law enforcement and employment-related AI systems.
key_obligations: Proposed only - not law. Tracked here for its signal value to India's AI legislative debate.

title: Digital India Act
issuing_body: Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology (MeitY)
summary: The long-anticipated successor to the IT Act 2000, expected to introduce risk-based classification of digital platforms and services, enhanced intermediary obligations, and dedicated provisions for AI and emerging technology including deepfakes and algorithmic transparency. Drafting discussions have been under way since 2023, and public consultation is anticipated in 2026. Tracked here because it would become the primary statutory home for AI regulation in India.
who_it_applies_to: If enacted: all digital platforms, intermediaries and AI services operating in India.
key_obligations: Details pending publication of a draft bill.

title: Strategy for AI in Healthcare for India (SAHI)
issuing_body: Ministry of Health and Family Welfare (MoHFW)
summary: MoHFW is developing a sector-specific Strategy for AI in Healthcare for India (SAHI), confirmed in the government's February 2026 healthcare-AI report. It is expected to consolidate governance of AI across diagnostics, clinical decision support and public health programmes, building on ICMR's 2023 ethical guidelines and the national AI Governance Guidelines. No draft has been published yet; this entry tracks the announcement.
who_it_applies_to: Once released: health-AI developers, hospitals, telemedicine platforms, and public health programmes deploying AI.
key_obligations: Details pending publication.
